title: Operating Expense: SG&A, R&D
subtitle: Operating costs - sitting between Gross Profit and Operating Income
openingQuestion: The CEO's salary, marketing expense, and office rent belong to which type of expense?
explanation: Operating expenses feed the organisation itself rather than directly making the product: sales salaries, marketing, management salaries, office rent, plus research and development. What's worth noticing is that they should be read differently: administrative costs growing faster than revenue signals a bloating organisation, while slashing R&D makes this year's profit look better by borrowing against future years.

realWorldExample.description: MWG is a textbook example of SG&A taking up a large share of a retailer's P&L: rent for thousands of stores, sales staff salaries, marketing, and supply-chain costs. During periods of weak consumer demand, MWG has had to actively close underperforming stores to cut SG&A, showing that operating leverage cuts both ways - margins improve quickly when revenue rises, but fixed SG&A eats into profit just as fast when revenue falls.

quiz.question: What does Operating Expense (OpEx) include?
options: SG&A, R&D, and depreciation - operating costs not tied directly to production
Only sales staff salaries and marketing expense for the period
Raw material costs and direct production labour wages
The company's entire cost base, including COGS and interest
quiz.explanation: OpEx = all operating costs other than COGS. It includes office salaries, marketing, R&D, depreciation, etc.

quiz.question: What does SG&A stand for?
options: Sales Growth & Advertising - the extra revenue gained from ad spending during the period
Selling (sales, marketing), General (shared salaries, office), Administrative (admin, legal)
Direct material and labour cost, i.e. the core of COGS
Interest expense and tax, sitting below the Operating Income line
quiz.explanation: SG&A = selling + general + administrative. It makes up most of OpEx at retail/service companies.

quiz.question: What is R&D?
options: Revenue & Distribution - the cost of shipping goods out to retailers and dealers during the period
Outsourced market-research spending, which always sits inside COGS
Research & Development - the cost of developing new products and improving existing ones
A capitalised investment that becomes an asset and never appears on the P&L
quiz.explanation: R&D = investment in the future. High at tech/pharma companies, low at retail/F&B.

quiz.question: A company has Gross Profit 600, OpEx 400. Operating Income = ?
options: 600 - OpEx has not been subtracted at this line yet
Cannot be calculated without knowing revenue

quiz.question: Is high OpEx good or bad?
options: It depends: high while revenue is flat eats into margin, high on R&D can be a good investment
Always bad - every dong of OpEx reduces the profit that belongs to shareholders
Always good - high OpEx shows the company is expanding scale quickly
No effect, since OpEx sits below the Operating Income line
quiz.explanation: High OpEx on marketing/sales builds future revenue. High OpEx on R&D builds future products. It isn't simply 'waste'.

quiz.question: If a company wants to improve its Operating Margin, what should it do?
options: Borrow more to expand, since interest expense is subtracted before Operating Income is calculated for the period
Grow revenue, cut unnecessary OpEx, or hold OpEx steady while revenue grows
Shrink revenue so the OpEx-to-revenue ratio looks smaller
Shift part of OpEx into COGS, since COGS doesn't affect the operating margin
quiz.explanation: Operating Margin = Operating Income / Revenue. Growing operating profit or revenue both improve the margin.

quiz.question: Company A: Revenue 1000, COGS 400, SG&A 300, R&D 100. Operating Income = ?
options: 600 (= 1,000 - 400, subtracting only COGS)
300 (= 1,000 - 400 - 300, dropping R&D by treating it as an investment)

quiz.question: Cutting R&D spending to boost Operating Income in the short run - good or bad?
options: Good - R&D isn't a mandatory cost, so cutting it is the right call
No effect, since R&D is capitalised and doesn't sit on this period's P&L
Good - cutting R&D raises both Operating Income and free cash flow over the long run
Bad - future products get weaker, trading long-term strength for short-term profit
quiz.explanation: Cutting R&D helps profit in the short term, but weakens the company's competitiveness and hurts it over the long run.

quiz.question: Why do accountants separate COGS from OpEx?
options: COGS varies with revenue while OpEx is nearly fixed - separating them lets you measure operating leverage
Because accounting standards ban combining the two cost types into one line
Because COGS is tax-deductible while OpEx is not, requiring different tax treatment
Because COGS belongs to the operating cash flow line while OpEx belongs to investing
quiz.explanation: COGS moves with revenue (variable). OpEx changes little (fixed). The split is used to plan for Operating Leverage.

quiz.question: Is high Operating Leverage (OpEx large relative to revenue) a good thing?
options: Always good, because high fixed costs help a company withstand a long downturn
Good when revenue is rising because margin improves quickly, dangerous when revenue falls
Always bad, because fixed costs remove flexibility across every business cycle
Unrelated to revenue - it only affects interest expense owed
quiz.explanation: High Operating Leverage: Revenue +10% → OI +20%. But Revenue -10% → OI -20%. Risk cuts in both directions.

quiz.question: Why is R&D often seen as an investment in the future rather than a pure expense, even though accounting still records it as Operating Expense for the current period?
options: Because regulation requires R&D to be recorded differently from every other operating cost
Because R&D always generates profit within the same period, so it doesn't need to be capitalised
Because R&D's future benefit is too uncertain to capitalise reliably, so it's expensed immediately
Because R&D doesn't affect Net Income, only the balance sheet
quiz.explanation: Accounting standards are conservative: because the future benefit of R&D is too uncertain to measure reliably, it's expensed immediately rather than capitalised as an asset the way CapEx is - even though, economically, R&D is really a long-term investment.

keyTakeaways: R&D = investment in the future, usually expensed right away
Operating Income = Gross Profit − SG&A − R&D

practicePrompt.question: A software company spends 2 billion/year on the engineering team writing new product code (R&D) and 3 billion/year on sales, marketing, and management (SG&A). Where do both of these sit on the P&L, and what is the fundamental difference between them?
options: Both sit inside COGS, since both are costs the company must incur to operate and sell its product
Both sit below Gross Profit as indirect operating costs; R&D is an investment in the future (usually expensed right away), while SG&A is the current cost of selling and managing the business
R&D is counted in COGS because it directly creates the product, while SG&A sits below Gross Profit as a separate item
There is no difference between R&D and SG&A - they're just two different names for the same type of cost
practicePrompt.explanation: SG&A = indirect operating cost (selling + administration). R&D = investment in the future, usually expensed right away. Both sit below Gross Profit and are subtracted to calculate Operating Income = Gross Profit − SG&A − R&D.

summary.commonMistake: Reading a concept as a phrase to memorise rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: R&D = investment in the future, usually expensed right away

application.title: Tell SG&A and R&D apart in a real financial statement
application.message: Open the financial statements of a technology or manufacturing company, find the SG&A and R&D lines, and read the notes (if available) to see whether the company is spending more on sales/management or on investing in its product.
application.secondary: The balance between these two items says a lot about a company's strategy.

sections.text: After Gross Profit, a business still has to pay for the machinery running behind the product: the sales team, management, research and development. This is Operating Expense (OpEx) - the second layer of cost on the Income Statement.

SG&A (Selling, General & Administrative) is indirect cost not tied directly to producing each unit, split into two groups: Selling (commissions, marketing, sales team salaries) and General & Administrative (leadership salaries, office rent, accounting, legal). Unlike COGS, SG&A doesn't rise and fall in proportion to units sold.
R&D: an investment in the future, an expense today

Research & Development is spending invested in future products/technology. Economically, R&D behaves more like a long-term investment than an operating cost, but under accounting standards most R&D still has to be expensed in the period it's incurred (aside from certain conditionally capitalised software cases).

Operating Income (often called EBIT) is the profit left after subtracting all SG&A and R&D from Gross Profit. This is a key metric for judging core operating efficiency, independent of how the company finances itself (debt or equity) and its applicable tax rate.

items: SG&A: selling + management cost, usually relatively fixed in the short run.
R&D: investment in future products, usually expensed right away under conservative accounting.
Operating Leverage: with fixed SG&A, rising revenue improves margin faster than proportionally.
Compare OpEx/Revenue ratios across companies in the same industry to judge operating efficiency.

sections.label: A warning sign when analysing
sections.text: A company growing revenue while SG&A grows even faster is a sign of losing control of costs, or of burning cash to win market share - worth examining closely before concluding anything about the quality of that growth.
